title: The same eighty-nine, sorted by sphere. The append (p. 21–40)
html:
Abhidhamma · Children’s Books

The same eighty-nine, sorted by sphere. The append (p. 21–40)

Pages 21–40 (20 pages)
Page 21

The same eighty-nine, sorted by sphere. The appendix to the book sorts the eighty-nine another way, by the bhūmi (sphere29) they belong to: 54 of the sense sphere, which make up ordinary life; 15 of the form sphere and 12 of the formless sphere, the jhāna (deep calm of mind) moments; and 8 lokuttara citta (consciousness beyond the world), the four path and four fruit moments that experience nibbāna (the end of all troubles). Five feelings. Every citta (consciousness) has a feeling with it. The appendix counts five: pleasant, unpleasant and indifferent mental feeling, and pleasant and unpleasant bodily feeling. Seeing and hearing arise with indifferent feeling. The gladness or sadness comes in the moments that follow. One process, all four kinds. The ancient texts describe what happens when a colour strikes the eye, moment by moment, in a vīthi (a process). Between processes there is a stream of bhavaṅga citta (life- continuum30 consciousness), which keeps the life going while nothing is being seen or heard or thought, as in dreamless sleep. These are vipāka (result). bhavaṅga K advert seeing receive investigate K determine G/B G/B G/B G/B javana G/B G/B G/B register bhavaṅga seven javana moments: good or bad; here kamma is made a colour strikes the eye V: vipāka (result) K: kiriya (functional) G/B: kusala or akusala (good or bad) one process at the eye-door, moment by moment “There is only one moment of consciousness (citta) at a time, and it falls away immediately after it has arisen, but it is succeeded by a next moment.” When a colour strikes the eye-sense, the stream of bhavaṅga (life-continuum) is interrupted, and these moments follow one another: 1. āvajjana (adverting31): a kiriya citta (functional consciousness) turns towards the object at the eyedoor. 2. cakkhu-viññāṇa (seeing): a vipāka citta (result consciousness) sees the colour. This is the only moment that sees. 3. sampaṭicchana (receiving) and santīraṇa (investigating): two more vipāka (result) moments take the object on. 4. votthapana (determining): a kiriya citta (functional consciousness) settles how the object will be taken. 5. javana (running): seven moments in a row of kusala citta (good consciousness) or akusala citta (bad consciousness). Here liking or disliking happens, and kamma (deed) is made. In an arahant (fully enlightened person) these seven are kiriya (functional). 6. tadārammaṇa (registering32): two vipāka (result) moments, and then the bhavaṅga (life-continuum) flows again. The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 21

Page 22

So in one process at the eye-door there are kiriya (functional), vipāka (result), and kusala (good) or akusala (bad) moments. Then a mind-door process follows, in which the colour is thought about and named. Only then does anyone know “a mango”. The seeing itself knew only colour. The whole thing is over in less than the blink of an eye, and it happens again and again, all day long, at every door. One at a time. Only one citta (consciousness) arises at a time. It arises, experiences one object, falls away33, and the next one arises. There is no second citta (consciousness) standing beside it to watch. There is only this moment, and then the next. A day in cittas. Hearing the cock crow: vipāka (result). Not wanting to get up: akusala (bad), rooted in lobha (attachment) to the warm bed. Getting up to help with the water jars: kusala (good). Seeing the sunrise: vipāka (result). Being absorbed in how beautiful it is: akusala (bad), as the book’s list says. Tasting the rice: vipāka (result). Wanting a second bowl: akusala (bad). Giving the second bowl to a younger brother: kusala (good). HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing 2. mental: to do with the mind 3. phenomena: things that happen or appear; here, the realities of mind and matter 4. experience: to know, see, hear or feel something; or the knowing itself 5. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought 6. mental factor: something that goes along with each moment of mind and does its own small job, such as feeling or remembering 7. morality: good conduct; not killing, not stealing, not lying and the rest 8. skilful: done well, with skill; here, good for the mind (unskilful: bad for the mind) 9. immoral: bad conduct; wrong 10. resultant: coming as a result 11. result: what comes later from a deed done before, as fruit comes from a seed 12. inoperative: not working as a cause; bringing no result 13. functional: doing a job without being a cause or a result 14. deed: something done; an act, good or bad 15. indifferent: neither pleasant nor unpleasant; in the middle 16. prompted: prompted: after some urging; unprompted: of one's own accord 17. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 18. generosity: giving freely and gladly 19. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being 20. restraint: holding oneself back from doing wrong 21. insight: seeing into something; here, seeing clearly for oneself that there is only mind and matter 22. meditation: developing the mind; people use this word in many different ways 23. tranquillity: calm; stillness of mind 24. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 25. ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really there 26. restlessness: not being able to be still; a mind that jumps about 27. process: a row of moments that follow one another in order 28. enlightenment: the moment when the truth is seen fully and for good, and the dirt of the mind is cut away 29. sphere: an area or level; here, a level of mind 30. life-continuum: the stream of mind that keeps life going when nothing is being seen, heard or thought, as in deep sleep 31. adverting: turning towards something 32. registering: taking note of 33. fall away: to end; to stop; to be gone The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 22

Page 23

Lesson 4: cetasika, the mental factors “kindness and hate cannot occur together at the same moment” The helpers. The other kind of nāma (mind) is the cetasika (mental factors1, or mental2 formations). The book says: “These mental factors arise3 accompanying each moment of experience4 (each citta). There is not one moment of experience occurring without at least some of them. Their function5 is to add to the experience each in their own way.” A citta (consciousness6) never arises alone. It comes with a company of mental factors, and together they make one moment of mind. Each has its own mark. “Each cetasika or mental factor has its own special characteristic7 by which it is recognised and function which it performs.” The book’s example is māna (conceit8): “the characteristic of conceit is haughtiness and self-praise is its function”. Conceit compares: “I am better”, or “I am worse”, or “I am just as good”. Whenever that mark appears, conceit is there, whatever name a person gives it. Fifty-two. “There are 52 different types of cetasikas.” The book names some: “feeling, perception9 (or memory), contact, intention10, attention, effort, interest, desire-to-do, restlessness11, attachment12, conceit, hate, envy13, awareness14, confidence15, detachment16, balance of mind, concentration17, kindness, compassion18.” The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 23

Page 24

citta consciousness phassa contact vedanā feeling saññā memory cetanā intention ekaggatā concentration jīvitindriya psychic life manasikāra attention the seven universals, with every citta universals with every moment particulars with some moments bad factors only in bad moments beautiful factors in every good moment abstinences right speech, action, livelihood illimitables compassion, sympathetic joy wisdom paññā mental factors in all “There are seven of these mental factors which occur with every moment of consciousness” They come in groups. Mental factors “arise with each moment of consciousness in groupings of certain types”. Some can never arise together. The book says: “kindness and hate cannot occur together at the same moment, restlessness and balance of mind cannot occur together, compassion and conceit cannot occur together”. A moment is either kind or angry; it cannot be both. People say “I love him but I am angry with him”, and that is true of a person over an afternoon, but never of one moment. The seven that are always there. Seven mental factors “occur with every moment of consciousness”. The book calls them “the universal19 cetasikas”. Pali English What it does phassa contact touches the object20, so that the moment meets it vedanā feeling feels the object as pleasant, unpleasant or neither saññā perception, or memory marks the object, so that it can be known again cetanā intention organises the moment and wills; when it is strong it is kamma (deed21) ekaggatā concentration holds the mind on the one object jīvitindriya psychic life22 keeps the moment alive for its brief time manasikāra attention turns the mind to the object Even in a moment of seeing there is contact with the colour, a feeling about it, a marking of it, an intention, a holding on it, a life, and an attention to it. The moment is gone before any of it can be noticed. The other groups. The book lists the rest, and its appendix gives every name. The 6 pakiṇṇaka (particulars), which “occur with particular states of consciousness” and not with all. They can be good or bad depending on the company they keep. The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 24

Page 25

Pali English vitakka initial application, applied thought vicāra sustained application adhimokkha determination23, decision viriya effort pīti interest, joy chanda desire-to-do The 14 akusala cetasika (bad mental factors), which “make up all the akusala moments of consciousness”. The first four are in every bad moment. Pali English moha ignorance24 ahirika lack of moral shame25 anottappa lack of fear of unwholesomeness26 uddhacca restlessness lobha attachment diṭṭhi wrong view27 māna conceit dosa aversion28, anger issā envy macchariya stinginess29 kukkucca regret, worry thīna sloth30 middha torpor31 vicikicchā doubt The 19 sobhana cetasika (beautiful mental factors), “so called because they are common to all morally32 beautiful moments of consciousness”. The first seven have names of their own; the other twelve come in six pairs, one for the mental factors and one for the citta (consciousness). Pali English saddhā confidence sati mindfulness33 hiri moral shame The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 25

Page 26

Pali English ottappa fear of unwholesomeness34 alobha disinterestedness35, non-attachment adosa amity36, non-hate tatramajjhattatā equanimity37, balance of mind passaddhi (composure38), a pair composure lahutā (lightness), a pair lightness mudutā (pliancy39), a pair pliancy kammaññatā (adaptability40), a pair adaptability pāguññatā (proficiency41), a pair proficiency ujukatā (rectitude42, straightness), a pair rectitude, straightness Then the 3 virati (abstinences43): sammā vācā (right speech), sammā kammanta (right action) and sammā ājīva (right livelihood44), which arise when a person holds back from a wrong word, a wrong deed or a wrong way of earning a living. The 2 appamaññā (illimitables45), “so called because their objects are without limit”: karuṇā (compassion) and muditā (sympathetic joy46). And “finally the last sobhana cetasika”: paññā (wisdom). With the nineteen, these make twenty-five beautiful factors, “arising in various combinations in the wholesome47 states of consciousness”. Seven and six and fourteen and nineteen and three and two and one make fifty-two. A moment of anger, taken apart. When a boy’s brother breaks his toy cart and anger arises, that one moment of akusala citta (bad consciousness) has with it the seven universals, some of the particulars, and from the fourteen bad factors at least these: dosa (anger) itself; moha (ignorance); ahirika (shamelessness) and anottappa (fearlessness of wrong), because at that moment there is no shame about being angry and no fear of where it leads; and uddhacca (restlessness). If the anger is at the brother for having a better cart, issā (envy) may be there. If it is anger at having to share, macchariya (stinginess) may be there. If afterwards there is fretting over having shouted, that is kukkucca (worry), in a later moment. All nineteen beautiful factors are absent. Kindness is a mental factor. Mettā (loving-kindness48) is not a person’s feeling; it is the mental factor adosa (non-hate), one of the nineteen beautiful ones, when it takes living beings49 as its object. Compassion is a mental factor. Confidence is a mental factor. So is envy, and so is laziness. None of them belongs to a person. Each arises when its conditions50 are present, does its work for one moment, and falls away51. A kind person is a person in whom kindness arises often. Why learn the names? Because the names make it possible to notice. When a child knows that there is a mental factor called issā (envy), whose mark is being unhappy at someone else’s good fortune, then the next time a friend wins a game and something sour arises, it can be known for what it is: not “me being horrible”, only issā (envy), a conditioned52 cetasika (mental factor), already falling away. The book says that the Abhidhamma “can lead us on to a better understanding of the practise of insight53“. The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 26

Page 27

HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. mental factor: something that goes along with each moment of mind and does its own small job, such as feeling or remembering 2. mental: to do with the mind 3. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 4. experience: to know, see, hear or feel something; or the knowing itself 5. function: the job that something does 6. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing 7. characteristic: the mark by which something is known; what is special about it 8. conceit: thinking oneself better than others, or worse, or just as good; pride that compares 9. perception: marking something in the mind so that it can be known again; remembering 10. intention: what the mind means to do; the mind's choosing 11. restlessness: not being able to be still; a mind that jumps about 12. attachment: wanting something and holding on to it; liking that will not let go 13. envy: being unhappy because someone else has something good 14. awareness: noticing what is really there right now; another word for mindfulness 15. confidence: trust in what is true and good; sureness 16. detachment: not holding on; letting go 17. concentration: keeping the mind on one thing 18. compassion: wanting to help someone who is suffering 19. universal: found in every one; here, mental factors that come with every moment of mind 20. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought 21. deed: something done; an act, good or bad 22. psychic life: the mental factor that keeps a moment of mind alive for its short time 23. determination: making up one's mind firmly and keeping to it 24. ignorance: not knowing; not understanding what is really there 25. moral shame: being ashamed to do wrong 26. fear of unwholesomeness: being afraid of the harm that doing wrong brings 27. wrong view: a wrong idea about what is real, such as the idea that there is a lasting self 28. aversion: not liking something and wanting it to go away; anger, even a little 29. stinginess: not wanting to give or share; meanness 30. sloth: laziness and dullness of mind 31. torpor: heaviness and sleepiness of mind 32. morality: good conduct; not killing, not stealing, not lying and the rest 33. mindfulness: noticing what is really there right now, without forgetting 34. unwholesome: bad for the mind: wanting, anger, not knowing 35. disinterestedness: not wanting anything for oneself 36. amity: friendliness 37. equanimity: an even, calm mind that is not shaken by good luck or bad 38. composure: calmness 39. pliancy: being soft and bendable, not stiff 40. adaptability: being able to fit to what is needed 41. proficiency: skill; being good at doing something 42. rectitude: straightness; being honest and right 43. abstain: to hold back from doing something, such as lying 44. livelihood: the way a person earns a living 45. illimitable: without limit; boundless 46. sympathetic joy: being glad when someone else is happy or does well 47. wholesome: good and healthy for the mind: giving, kindness, patience, understanding 48. loving-kindness: wishing others well; friendliness to everyone 49. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being 50. condition: something that has to be there before another thing can happen 51. fall away: to end; to stop; to be gone 52. conditioned: made to happen by other things; it could not come up on its own 53. insight: seeing into something; here, seeing clearly for oneself that there is only mind and matter The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 27

Page 28

Quiz 2 (lessons 3 and 4) The answers are at the back. 1. How many kinds of citta (consciousness) does the Abhidhamma count, and in how many classes? (a) 52 kinds in 7 classes (b) 89 kinds in 4 classes (c) 28 kinds in 2 classes (d) 31 kinds in 3 classes 2. Put the four classes of citta (consciousness) in order, from the fewest kinds to the most. kusala citta (good consciousness), 21 kiriya citta (functional consciousness), 20 akusala citta (bad consciousness), 12 vipāka citta (result consciousness), 36 3. Which of these is on the book’s list of examples of akusala citta (bad consciousness)? (a) being bored (b) bowing to a teacher (c) holding back from a lie (d) seeing a beautiful colour 4. Seeing a pleasant colour: is that kusala (good), akusala (bad) or vipāka (result)? Why? 5. Which feeling always goes with citta (consciousness) rooted in dosa (anger)? (a) pleasant feeling (b) indifferent feeling (c) unpleasant feeling (d) any of the three 6. What does kiriya citta (functional consciousness) mean, and when does it arise? 7. The book says one mental factor has “haughtiness” as its characteristic and “self-praise” as its function. Which? (a) issā (envy) (b) māna (conceit) (c) dosa (anger) (d) uddhacca (restlessness) 8. Name the seven universal cetasika (mental factors), which arise with every moment of consciousness. 9. True or false: kindness and hate can arise together in one moment of consciousness. 10. How many cetasika (mental factors) are there in all? (a) 7 (b) 28 (c) 52 (d) 89 11. Which mental factor is mettā (loving-kindness), according to the Abhidhamma? The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 28

Page 29

Lesson 5: rūpa, matter “The four great elements always arise with those rupas which are known as the derived rupas.” Twenty-eight. The third conditioned1 reality2 is rūpa (matter3). The book says: “There are 28 classes of rupa, 16 being classified4 as subtle5 and 12 as gross6.” Gross means the kinds that strike the senses directly: the five sense organs and the seven objects7 that can be seen, heard, smelt, tasted or touched. Subtle means the finer kinds. The four great elements. At the base of all matter are the four mahābhūta (great elements8). The book gives them with their real meanings: 1. paṭhavī dhātu (the element of earth), or solidity9 2. āpo dhātu (the element of water), or cohesion10 3. tejo dhātu (the element of fire), or temperature 4. vāyo dhātu (the element of wind), or motion These are not the earth in the garden, the water in the well, the fire on the hearth and the wind in the trees. They are qualities. Earth is hardness and softness. Water is the holding together of the parts. Fire is heat and cold. Wind is motion and pressure. A stone has all four: it is hard, it holds together, it has a temperature, and it presses on the hand that holds it. So does a drop of water, and so does the body. A thing is never only “earth”; it is a group in which one element is strongest. The elements in the body. In the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta (the Discourse11 on the Analysis of the Elements), the Buddha taught a young man called Pukkusāti, in a potter’s workshop, to see his own body as the four elements. What is hard in the body is the earth element: the hair, the nails, the teeth, the skin, the flesh, the bones, and the rest. What is fluid and holds together is the water element: blood, sweat, tears, and the rest. The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 29

Page 30

What warms the body and digests what is eaten is the fire element. What moves in the body, the breath going in and out, is the wind element. And of each he taught: this is not mine, this is not what I am, this is not my self. The earth element inside the body and the earth element in a rock are the same element. The derived kinds. “The four great elements always arise12 with those rupas which are known as the derived13 rupas.” Derived means depending on the four, as a pot depends on clay. The book names them: “the physical sense-organs of eye-sense, ear-sense, taste-sense, etc., and the sense-objects of colour, sound, smell and flavour”. The eye-sense is not the eyeball; it is the fine matter inside the eye that can be struck by colour. Then there are “the male or female characteristic14, heart-base, nutritive15 essence (food), space, lightness, bodily intimation16, speech intimation, etc.” Bodily intimation is the matter by which the body makes its meaning known, as when a hand beckons. Speech intimation is the matter by which speech makes its meaning known. The heart-base is the matter on which most kinds of citta (consciousness17) depend, as seeing depends on the eye-sense. paṭhavī earth: solidity āpo water: cohesion tejo fire: temperature vāyo wind: motion the four great elements (4) the derived kinds (24), which always arise with the four 5 sense organs: eye, ear, nose, tongue, body 4 sense objects: colour, sound, smell, flavour heart-base · nutritive essence · life · male and female (5) space · bodily intimation · speech intimation (3) lightness, pliancy, wieldiness · arising, continuity, decay, impermanence (7) 4 + 24 = 28 kinds of rūpa (matter); 12 gross, 16 subtle “All that matter consists of is these 28 different types of rupa in different combinations.” All matter. The book says: “All that matter consists of is these 28 different types of rupa in different combinations.” A mountain, a mango, a hand, a sound, a smell: twenty-eight kinds, in groups. Rūpa does not know. Rūpa (matter) does not experience18 anything. In the last lesson of the book: “Hardness is a type of rupa (matter). It cannot know anything about anything.” The hardness of a bench does not know that someone is sitting on it. The colour of a face does not know that it is seen. When a person says “the bench is hard”, there are two realities: hardness, which is rūpa (matter), and the experience of hardness through the body-sense19, which is nāma (mind). The eightfold group. Rūpa (matter) never arises as a single kind. The appendix to the book says that matter “consists of 8 basic constituents20 which compose all matter”, the suddhaṭṭhaka kalāpa (the pure eightfold group): the four great elements and four derived from them. Pali English paṭhavī solidity āpo cohesion The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 30

Page 31

Pali English tejo temperature vāyo motion vaṇṇa colour gandha smell rasa taste ojā nutriment Where there is hardness there is also colour, smell, taste and nutriment, whether anyone notices them or not. The appendix then lists “a further 20 types of matter, all of which are also derived rupas”: the five sense organs; the male and female characteristic, which counts as two; the heart base; the material21 lifeprinciple; space; bodily intimation; speech intimation; sound; lightness, plasticity and adaptability22; and growth, continuity, decay and impermanence23. “The fourteenth type, male and female characteristic, is of two types which makes a total of 28 rupas.” Groups of matter in the body arise from four sources: from kamma (deeds24), from citta (consciousness), from temperature and from food. The eye-sense and the heart-base are produced by kamma (deeds). The movement of the hand that beckons is produced by citta (consciousness). Rūpa falls away. Matter lasts longer than mind, but not long. The ancient texts say that one group of rūpa (matter) lasts as long as seventeen moments of citta (consciousness), and then it is gone, and another group has taken its place. The body that sat down is not the body that stands up. The five khandhas. The ancient texts have one more way of sorting everything met in Lessons 3, 4 and 5. The appendix to the book calls them the five khandha (aggregates25, or groups), “the aggregates of our daily existence”: 1. rūpa-khandha (the group of matter): all twenty-eight kinds of rūpa (matter), “hardness, temperature, pressure, colour, smell, taste” 2. vedanā-khandha (the group of feeling): the mental factor26 feeling, in its five kinds 3. saññā-khandha (the group of perception27, or memory): the mental28 factor that “marks the object of experience so that it can be recognised now and in the future” 4. saṅkhāra-khandha (the group of mental formations): “the other fifty cetasikas” 5. viññāṇa-khandha (the group of consciousness): “all types of citta” The appendix says: “The khandhas are called the ‘groups of grasping29‘. This means that we cling30 to, or grasp at these aggregates as belonging to a self. As long as we take them for self we do not understand them as they really are, just paramattha dhammas, just conditioned realities.” When the nun31 Vajirā said, in the Introduction, that “when the aggregates are present ‘sentient32 being33’ is the convention34 we use”, these five groups were what she meant. HARD WORDS IN THIS CHAPTER 1. conditioned: made to happen by other things; it could not come up on its own 2. reality: something that is really there, not only a name or an idea The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 31

Page 32

3. matter: the kind of reality that does not know or feel anything, such as hardness, colour or sound 4. classification: sorting things into kinds 5. subtle: fine, faint and hard to notice 6. gross: here, coarse and easy to notice; not 'disgusting' 7. object: the thing that a moment of mind knows: a colour, a sound, a thought 8. element: one of the basic parts that everything is made of 9. solidity: hardness or softness; being solid 10. cohesion: holding together; the sticking-together of the parts 11. discourse: a talk or sermon; here, one of the Buddha's talks written down 12. arise: to come up; to begin; to happen 13. derived: coming from something else and depending on it 14. characteristic: the mark by which something is known; what is special about it 15. nutriment: food; what feeds the body and keeps it going 16. intimation: a sign that makes a meaning known, as a nod or a word does 17. consciousness: a moment of mind that knows something, such as seeing or hearing 18. experience: to know, see, hear or feel something; or the knowing itself 19. bodysense: the sense of touch, all over the body 20. constituent: a part that something is made of 21. material: made of matter; the stuff that does not know anything 22. adaptability: being able to fit to what is needed 23. impermanent: not lasting; passing away 24. deed: something done; an act, good or bad 25. aggregate: a group or heap of things taken together 26. mental factor: something that goes along with each moment of mind and does its own small job, such as feeling or remembering 27. perception: marking something in the mind so that it can be known again; remembering 28. mental: to do with the mind 29. grasping: holding on tightly; clinging 30. clinging: holding on tightly; not wanting to let go 31. nun: a woman who has left home to follow the Buddha's rule of life 32. sentient: able to feel and know; alive and aware 33. being: any living creature: a person, an animal, a heavenly being 34. conventional: the ordinary everyday way of talking, as when a pile of parts is called a chariot The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 32

Page 33

Lesson 6: kamma and vipāka, deeds and their results “Moral action, whenever performed, will always bring a pleasant result at some time in the future.” Seeing is a result. The book says: “Whenever we see, hear, taste, smell or touch an object1, that experience2, as was mentioned before, is resultant3-consciousness4 (vipaka-citta). It is the result5 of a deed6 performed at some time in the past.” A pleasant sight is the result of a good deed; an unpleasant sound is the result of a bad one. Nobody chooses what will strike the eye and the ear in the next moment. “The area of cause and result (kamma and vipaka) is most important in Abhidhamma. To sort out experience into cause and result can cast our lives into a much clearer perspective7.” the deed cetanā (intention), strong enough to act kamma the cause some time later: this life, the next, or a life far away. “We don't know when.” vipāka the result: seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching a pleasant or unpleasant object “It is the result of a deed performed at some time in the past.” Twenty kinds of deed. “The Buddha enumerated8 ten types of moral9 and skillful10 action and ten types of immoral11 or unskillful action through body, speech or mind. Moral action, whenever performed, will always bring a pleasant result at some time in the future. Immoral action will always bring an unpleasant result.” The ten akusala kamma (bad deeds) are: The Abhidhamma for Young Readers · 33

Page 34

Through Pali English body pāṇātipāta killing body adinnādāna stealing body kāmesu micchācāra sexual misconduct12 (being unfaithful to a husband or wife) speech musāvāda lying speech pisuṇā vācā slandering13 speech pharusā vācā rude speech speech samphappalāpa frivolous14 talk mind abhijjhā covetousness15, wanting what belongs to others mind vyāpāda ill will16 mind micchā diṭṭhi wrong view17 The book says: “These ten types of action whenever performed, no matter what the justification18 that we make for them, are always immoral actions and capable of producing an unpleasant result.” It gives examples of things people excuse: killing insects, cheating on taxes, abusive19 speech. And about killing: “the Buddha pointed out that destruction of other being’s lives is never to the welfare of oneself or the other being. The justification for killing is just thinking, but the actual moment of killing is always immoral and never to anybody’s benefit.” Ten kinds of good deed. What kamma really is. Kamma (deed) is not a law outside a person, and not a ledger kept somewhere. The book says: “Kamma (or karma) can also be understood more precisely as the cetasika or mental factor31 called intention32 (cetana). When intention motivates one of the ten types of moral or immoral actions through body, speech or mind then it is called kamma because it is strong enough to produce a result at some time in the future.” So kamma (deed) is cetanā (intention) grown strong enough to act. Results in a life. The book lists the unpleasant things that come to everyone: “sickness, disease, accidents”; people who “abuse us” or “misrepresent35 us”; “our bodies wear out”. And the pleasant things: “we meet friendly people, we receive gifts, we have a strong body, we have good eyesight, we have a beautiful partner, we live in a pleasant house with beautiful children. All of these things happen to us because of deeds performed at some time in the past, we don’t know when.” People arrange their lives around the pleasant results they hope for: “we want a nice house, we want peace and quiet”, “we look forward to delicious, well-prepared food. But these things come to us only because of moral deeds we have performed in the past.” Then the book draws the conclusion. “The only way to receive more of this is not to climb over the next man, not to cheat on tax, not to lie about our qualifications36, not to abuse other people, but to be kind, respectful, generous, honest and upright37 in character. The Buddha taught quite clearly that it is deeds in the past that determine our life situation right now.” Not knowing when. A good deed does not bring its result at once. The result may come in this life, in the next, or in a life far away. The deed is a seed; the result is the fruit; and between them there may be a long time. Every moment of seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching is a fruit of some seed planted before. Two moments to tell apart. Suppose a boy hears a rude word. The hearing is vipāka (result): the fruit of a past deed, and nothing can be done about it now. What comes next is not result. If anger arises, that is akusala citta (bad consciousness), a new seed. If patience arises, that is kusala citta (good consciousness), a new seed of a different kind. The moment of result is closed; the moment after it is open. Lesson 7: the wheel of birth and death “Nay, to supply them all, the straw, boughs, twigs and leaves in this India would come to an end and be used up, ere this were done.” A wheel, not a ladder. “Birth and death are dealt with in minute detail in the Abhidhamma.” The book says: “The Buddha taught that life or existence is a cyclic process1 with beings2 dying and passing on to other existences according to their moral3 and immoral4 deeds5.” Some teachings say that a being can never be born into a worse life than its present one, as if life were a ladder that only goes up. The Buddha did not teach that. “The Buddha maintains that life, far from being necessarily progressive, can for many beings be a destructive and downward process. He likens it a wheel turning around and around with no end to it. Beings are ever repeating mistakes or performing deeds due to their ignorance6 of the way things are which will bring them more and more unhappiness in the future.” The ancient texts call this wheel saṃsāra (the round of births).
